Find the points where the circle ${x}^{2}+(y+4)^{2}=20$ intersects the line $x-3y=2$ (sketched above).
worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation $x-3y=2,$ as follows:

$$
y=\frac{x}{3}-\frac{2}{3}
$$

To find $x$-coordinates of the intersection points, we need to substitute $y=\frac{x}{3}-\frac{2}{3}$ into the equation of the circle and solve the resulting equation for $x:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+(y+4)^{2} & =20 \\ {x}^{2}+{(\frac{x}{3}-\frac{2}{3}+4)}^{2} & =20 \\ {x}^{2}+{(\frac{x}{3}+\frac{10}{3})}^{2} & =20 \\ {x}^{2}+\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{20x}{9}+\frac{100}{9} & =20 \\ \frac{10{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{20x}{9}+\frac{100}{9} & =20 \\ {x}^{2}+2x+10 & =18 \\ {x}^{2}+2x-8 & =0 \\ (x+4)(x-2) & =0 \\ x & =-4,2.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the $y$-coordinates of the intersection points, we need to substitute $x=-4,2$ into the equation of the line and compute $y$-values. Start with $x=-4$:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{x}{3}-\frac{2}{3} \\  & =-\frac{4}{3}-\frac{2}{3} \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the first intersection point is $(-4,-2).$ Next, we plug in $x=2$:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{x}{3}-\frac{2}{3} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}-\frac{2}{3} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second intersection point is $(2,0).$

Therefore, the line $x-3y=2$ intersects the circle ${x}^{2}+(y+4)^{2}=20$ at the points $(-4,-2)$ and $(2,0).$
